abstract: Background: Complex diseases with a high genetic component often cluster in families and are associated with quantitative traits (QT-s) such as endophenotypes showing comorbidity with the end-point disease trait. Detecting associations with such QT-s can provide a non-invasive approach to indicate disease onset at an early stage, or help in tracking disease severity. Traditional case-control studies generally involve unrelated individuals, which can introduce heterogeneity due to varying lifestyle and exposure patterns. Often QT values may be available from related individuals such as families of affected probands. In these situations, assessment of comorbidity restricting to unrelated cases and controls leads to unnecessary loss of power. On the other hand, ignoring the correlation structure of families leads to grossly incorrect confidence intervals impacting both type 1 error and power of tests. Yet, these practices are common in the absence of standard inference procedures for such data. Methods: We propose statistical procedures for analyzing clustered data to infer association between the QT-s and the binary trait. The methods allow a mix of families and unrelated cases and utilizes all available individuals. In particular, two novel competing approaches are proposed and evaluated: a parametric approach based on multivariate normal likelihood and a non-parametric approach that combines the Wilcoxon rank-sum test with a modified version of the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Results: We conducted simulation studies to assess type 1 error and power across multiple scenarios, which demonstrated the robustness of the proposed tests. Both the tests perform considerably better than both the classical t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test under both parametric and non-parametric settings. We illustrate the proposed methods by applying them on sibship data from the Centre for Brain and Mind program to identify a number of quantitative precursors significantly associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder. Conclusion: In summary, the proposed methods provide a robust and powerful approach to detect comorbid endophenotypes incorporating data from families of affected individuals. Findings from the analysis of sibling-based data on schizophrenia and bipolar disorder support role of a few selected neurocognitive assessments as potential markers of these disorders.
